F1. Checking is required, with substantial discretion over measures and acceptance standards. Both maps expect AI outputs to be tested before use, monitored, re-tested on change and reviewed by people where the stakes are high, while leaving important choices about references, metrics and acceptance thresholds to providers and deploying bodies, subject to applicable duties. The AI Act requires that testing of high-risk systems "shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds" appropriate to a purpose the provider itself defines (EU046, Art. 9(8)), and that providers state "the level of accuracy, including its metrics" in the instructions they give deployers (Art. 13(3)(b)(ii)). EDPS guidance tells organisations buying a system that they "should request from the provider a set of metrics that will allow for the evaluation of the AI system against the organisation’s objectives" (EDPS_AI_risk, s. 5.2.5). In the UK, the Playbook tells bodies "You must be clear about what objective measures you’re assessing the AI outputs against" without naming any (UK174), and the transparency guidance asks them to "describe any bias and fairness evaluation you have undertaken" (UK086, s. 10) rather than to meet a standard. Where thresholds appear, the organisation sets them: deployment gates should block releases "that exceed acceptable bias levels" (AI_Insights). Illustrative output thresholds include "> 80% of sampled outputs rated acceptable by human reviewers" (UK071), and one case study's "accuracy threshold of 80%" (UK174). Some provisions are more specific: the Article 50 guidelines make "Fact-checking the accuracy of the content" the minimum for a human review that exempts AI-generated text from labelling (EU_Art50, para. 134), and the transparency Code sets what a test of watermark detection must show (EU121). Article 15(2) also requires the Commission, with relevant stakeholders, to encourage as appropriate the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies. Discretion therefore operates within substantive obligations and arrangements for further measurement guidance; it is not an unrestricted choice of any convenient test.

F2. Stability and configuration are addressed unevenly across duties and guidance. The AI Act says testing "shall ensure that high-risk AI systems perform consistently for their intended purpose" (EU046, Art. 9(6)) and asks them to "perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle" (Art. 15(1)), without specifying a repeated-run agreement statistic in those provisions. Article 15(2) also provides for encouraging benchmarks and measurement methodologies. EU documents mention prompts and configuration mainly as questions of data protection and responsibility: staff must not share non-public information or personal data with an online generative AI model (EC_staff_GenAI_2023, Rule 1); for the EDPS, the body that "defines the prompts and system configurations" determines the means of processing (EDPS_GenAI_orientations), and the Court of Auditors plans a prompt library "with appropriate quality controls and documentation" (ECA_strategy). Explicit repeated- or similar-prompt checks appear in the UK guidance examined here. The audit offices' catalogue says: "Output consistency: test for consistent outputs by running the same prompt multiple times, especially for generative models" (UK268), the testing framework asks teams to "Check whether the model gives inconsistent or unexplained outputs when given similar prompts" (UK071), and AI Insights asks for consistency between environments. These passages do not prescribe a common repeated-run agreement statistic or a specific response to each observed disagreement. This does not displace general duties to address risks or justify suitability. The testing framework also gives an illustrative perturbation measure, “Stability: prediction variance ≤ 1% under perturbations” (UK071). The transparency template lets bodies leave the model specification blank for off-the-shelf models they have not "trained, validated, tested, or applied any refinement techniques to" (UK087).

F3. Oversight duties are supplemented by guidance on review triggers, reviewer capability and testing. The Playbook calls for validation of high-risk decisions, meaningful intervention, assessment of review stages and mechanisms for users to report problems that prompt review (UK174). Review triggers can therefore depend on the use, output characteristics and reported problems. AI Insights describes routing uncertain or sensitive outputs to trained reviewers. DWP and Commission staff guidance ask users to check outputs for inaccuracies and bias (UK190; EC_staff_GenAI_2023). UK071 goes further: it recommends testing handover triggers and override mechanisms, and testing with non-technical users whether they can identify hallucinations, bias or off-topic outputs. The transparency template asks when and how review occurs and how it is assessed or assured (UK087). In the EU, Article 14 addresses effective oversight, anomaly detection, automation bias, interpretation, override and intervention; Article 26(2) requires competence, training, authority and support. Article 14(5) requires separate verification by two people for the specified remote-biometric systems, with an express proportionality exception for specified law-enforcement, migration, border-control or asylum uses. Article 50(4) and its guidance provide a different, use-specific arrangement: substantive human review or editorial control and editorial responsibility can exempt published public-interest AI text from disclosure. The guidelines require knowledgeable substantive examination and fact checking, and reject merely superficial approval (EU_Art50, paras 133–135). These duties and recommendations address more than the presence of a reviewer. Organisations retain important choices about how review is implemented and evaluated, and the documents do not demonstrate its effectiveness in practice. The experiment examines hypothetical score-based routing, not reviewer performance.

F4. The sampled UK documents emphasise deploying bodies; the EU sample combines provider regulation with deployer duties. The sampled UK guidance asks bodies to assess whether and how to use AI, within existing legal duties. The Playbook tells bodies to "Adopt a risk-based approach to the use of AI and consider whether it’s appropriate to use AI in high-risk applications" (UK174), and DSIT's assurance guidance lets "low-risk use-cases" rely on fewer assurance techniques than high-risk ones (UK206). Standard-setting is passed down to organisations and regulators, and the firm rules include existing law, the Secure by Design principles, "ten mandatory principles for central government" (UK266), DWP's own policy (UK190) and the transparency standard, which governs publication rather than use (UK085, UK086). In the EU sample, the AI Act places substantial system-design and conformity duties on providers before market entry (EU046, Arts 9–15 and 43). Public bodies appear as deployers that must use systems "in accordance with the instructions for use" (Art. 26(1)), register their use (Art. 49(3)), carry out and notify a fundamental rights impact assessment (Art. 27), inform people (Art. 26(11)) and explain decisions on request (Art. 86). EU institutions' guidance for their own use of AI, from the EDPS, the European Parliament and the Commission, follows the UK pattern: it governs the body that uses the tool. Part of this contrast reflects the level and scope of the sampled instruments (section 4.2); it is not an exhaustive account of either legal system.

F5. External assessment and approval depend on the system and its use. Conformity assessment of a system and independent authorisation of a public body’s particular use are distinct. Article 43(2) provides for internal-control assessment for high-risk systems in Annex III points 2–8, while some biometric systems involve a notified body and sectoral product rules provide other assessment routes (Art. 43(1), (3)). The sample also identifies use-specific authorisation and consultation requirements. Police use of real-time remote biometric identification "must be authorized by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority prior to its use" (EU043, para. 382), and post-remote identification needs authorisation "ex ante, or without undue delay and no later than 48 hours" (EU046, Art. 26(10)). Where data-protection risks cannot be reduced, EU institutions "would have to prior consult the EDPS" (EDPS_AI_risk) and UK bodies "must consult the ICO before you can start processing personal data" (UK174). Where no separate use-authorisation requirement applies, the deployer still has its own duties and must "suspend the use of that system" if it has reason to consider that it presents a risk (EU046, Art. 26(5)). A provider relying on Article 6(3) for an Annex III system must assess the conditions, document its conclusion and meet the relevant registration requirements (Art. 6(4)). Recital 53 gives incoming-document classification as a possible narrow procedural task, but the exception also requires no significant risk, including no material influence on decision outcomes; profiling of natural persons remains high-risk. It is not an automatic exemption for topic classifiers. In the EU, authorities can act after the event: a market surveillance authority can re-evaluate a provider's classification of a system as not high-risk (Art. 80(1)) and require it "to withdraw the AI system from the market, or to recall it" (Art. 79(2)). Apart from ICO consultation and central spend approvals (UK174), which concern data protection and spending rather than whether the tool works, the cited UK guidance also describes internal approval: before go-live, "for high-risk AI, this may require senior approval or an ethics board decision" (UK071), and AI Insights asks for a manager's written approval before a user-built agent is deployed. Few UK documents say who decides to stop using a model. In AI Insights the knowledge and information management team decides when a model is "relevant and accurate enough", and "users could turn off the model" (AI_Insights); in an EHRC worked example a police force suspends its own use (UK216).

F6. Resource duties coexist with shared support; capacity in practice is not established. The documents combine organisational responsibilities for resourcing assurance with shared guidance, training, expertise and targeted funding. The Playbook describes free Civil Service Learning and Government Campus resources and points to Government Office for Technology Transfer support and funding for government-wide solutions (UK174). UK139 records an announced £10 million package for regulator capability; it does not establish disbursement or funding for deploying bodies’ particular assurance checks. The AI Opportunities Action Plan recommends central finance and tools to scale successful pilots (UK082, Recommendation 39) and cites £21 million for twelve NHS imaging networks covering 66 trusts as a deployment-funding example (Recommendation 40), not an assurance budget. The AI Act provides for an impact-assessment questionnaire template (Art. 27(5)), training and advice arrangements for deployers and, as appropriate, local public authorities (Art. 62), and expert support for Member States’ enforcement work (Art. 69). Article 70(3) requires adequate technical, financial and human resources for national competent authorities and annual reassessment; Article 70(6) requires periodic reporting on resource adequacy. These recipients and purposes differ from resources available to each deploying body. Deployers also face support and staffing expectations for oversight (Art. 26(2); EU121). UK268 and UK071 provide practical guidance on consistency testing. The documents identify resource duties and support arrangements but do not establish actual access, uptake or sufficiency, or whether dedicated funding or staff for the experiment’s checks are available in practice.

F7. Consequences vary by duty, actor and legal route; enforcement in practice is not established. The UK sources describe different potential consequences: DWP non-compliance and failure to report security incidents can lead to disciplinary action (UK190); Ofgem identifies existing sectoral enforcement powers, including penalties of up to 10% of a regulated person’s turnover, redress and orders for relevant breaches (UK010); contracts can allocate supplier consequences (UK099); and EHRC warns that public bodies may face reputational damage and legal action under the Equality Act 2010 and the Public Sector Equality Duty (UK216). These are not automatic penalties for an incorrect AI output. The ATRS scope document does not specify a distinct sanction for failure to publish (UK085); this does not establish that non-compliance has no legal or administrative consequences. Under the AI Act, Member States determine the extent of administrative fines on their public authorities and bodies (Art. 99(8)). Union institutions can face EDPS fines up to EUR 1 500 000 for prohibited practices and EUR 750 000 for other requirements or obligations (Art. 100). These are legal maxima, not observed fines. Article 111(2), as amended (EU_Omnibus), contains a 2 August 2030 compliance provision for the relevant existing high-risk systems intended for public-authority use, within transitional rules that address significant design changes and preserve the application of Article 5. It is not a blanket postponement of all obligations for public-sector AI. The sample does not include Member States’ national implementing rules or establish enforcement frequency or effectiveness.

F8. Public transparency and supervisory accountability coexist, with different disclosure and challenge arrangements. UK ATRS records name an accountable role rather than an individual (UK086) and describe review or appeal arrangements. Existing legal and regulatory routes also remain relevant. The EU combines notifications to supervisors and documentation supplied on request with public-facing mechanisms: database information is generally public, subject to the specified exceptions (Arts 49, 71); Article 85 provides a complaint route; and Article 86 provides a right to explanation for specified adversely affecting decisions based on relevant Annex III systems, subject to its conditions. The non-public registration arrangements for specified law-enforcement, migration, asylum and border-control uses should not be generalised to the whole database. Providers and deployers have different, potentially overlapping responsibilities; UK bodies also retain responsibilities when buying tools (UK174). The analysis identifies formal disclosure, scrutiny and challenge arrangements, not their use or effectiveness in practice.
